The correct answer is C, catastrophising. Catastrophising is a cognitive distorition where a person views a situation as being much worse than it actually is. This is common in anxiety and depression. Arbitrary interferences is where a person believes that a minor event has a major effect e.g. 'I got a B in that test so I will fail every tests at uni'. Black and white thinking is where a person sees things as either good or bad with no in between e.g. 'I either get the grades or I'm a failure'. Personalising is where a person sees things as being their fault when in fact there are other reasons e.g. 'I didn't get the grades because I'm not smart enough'. Selective thinking is where a person only focuses on things that confirm their existing beliefs e.g. 'I didn't get into my first choice uni, of course I didn't get into that course I want to study'.

C is the correct answer! Natural killer cells are not sentry cells, but are instead a type of cytotoxic lymphocyte that attack cells that are already inside the body, such as virally infected cells.  A sentinel cell is a cell that acts as a sentry, meaning it is one of the first cells of the immune system to encounter a pathogen. This allows the immune system to detect the pathogen early and mount a response.  Sentinal cells have 'pattern recognition receptors' (PRRs) on their surface, which recognise 'pathogen associated molecular patterns' (PAMPs) on the surface of pathogens. When a PRR is bound by a PAMP, it triggers a response, which can include the release of a secreted chemical called a 'cytokine'.  Sentinal cells include:Dendritic cellsE.g. found in the skin and are responsible for 'sampling' the environment for pathogens. When detected, they release cytokines and migrate to the nearest lymph node to present their 'captured' antigen to a helper T cell. This helper T cell will then proliferate and differentiate into a CD122 cell, which will then travel back to the site of infection to stimulate the cytotoxic T cells to attack the pathogen.MacrophagesE.g. found in the liver and spleen. Also detect pathogens by PRRs and release cytokines.E.g. TNF-alpha, IL-1 and IL-6, which can cause systemic symptoms of inflammation, such as fever.

However, a straight leg raise is usually a different test to spinal cord compression - it is positive in only half of cases of spinal cord compression and is worse in spinal stenosis than spinal cord compression.

The correct answer is the Quadruple Test. This is because this woman is obese, and it is recognised that obesity is a risk factor for false positive results in the Quadruple Test. The Quadruple Test measures the levels of four different hormones in the maternal serum: AFP, β-hCG, ue3 and Inhibin A.  Of the other options:Amniocentesis and CVS are both diagnostic tests, not screening tests. They are not affected by maternal obesity. The Combined Test measures the levels of β-hCG and maternal serum PAPP-A. It is the most accurate screening test, but is rarely used as the Quadruple Test is cheaper and is accurate enough.  NIFTY is a non-invasive screening test that measures cell-free DNA in the mother's blood. It is not affected by obesity.  Source: 'Screening and Diagnostic Testing in Pregnancy' lecture, Case 7

D is the correct answer. Clozapine is an atypical antipsychotic that is known to cause agranulocytosis, a serious side effect where white blood cells of the granulocyte type are drastically reduced, often due to bone marrow suppression. This can result in life-threatening infections due to the decreased ability of the immune system to fight off pathogens. Other cell types may also be affected, but aDNAV is specifically associated with granulocytes. Other cell types that can be affected by drugs include B lymphocytes (lymphopenia), monocytes, eosinophils and neutrophils. Serious reactions that are linked to other drugs include cholestatic jaundice (e.g. domperidone), hepatotoxicity (e.g. risperidone), QT interval prolongation (e.g. citalopram), and serotonin syndrome (e.g. SSRIs and TCAs).
